forces.title: AI-driven workforce transformation redefines GCC operating models.
forces.description: AI is fundamentally reshaping GCCs, projecting 25-35% headcount reduction in 3 years and 55-65% in 5-10 years while multiplying economic value per person by 3-5x. This structural shift moves GCCs from execution centers to "Global Intelligence Centres," focusing on judgment, accountability, and AI governance. Leaders must pivot from headcount-driven models to value creation, or risk strategic irrelevance. This transformation is deliberate and phased, moving from silent restructuring to structural compression and reconstitution.

forces.title: Onshoring risk grows as AI enables GCC output with fewer people.
forces.description: The significant productivity gains from AI within GCCs, potentially reducing headcount by 55-65% for the same output, raises the question of whether parent companies might opt to 'onshore' these functions. However, India's large tech workforce (over 2 million in GCCs, millions more in broader tech) is accumulating deep AI deployment experience, making it difficult for other geographies to match. GCC leaders must actively articulate this unique value proposition to headquarters to mitigate this potential onshoring risk effectively.

forces.title: AI adoption and cloud modernization fuel GCC expansion.
forces.description: India's IT sector is experiencing strong hiring growth (16% YoY in April 2025) driven by AI adoption, cloud modernization, and the expansion of Global Capability Centres. The GCC workforce is projected to reach 3.46 million by 2030, supported by the rapid integration of AI across various roles, indicating a significant tailwind for the sector's growth and employment opportunities. This sustained demand for advanced tech skills positions GCCs favorably in India's evolving digital landscape.

forces.title: Increased BFSI spending and GenAI boost IT services, benefiting GCCs.
forces.description: The IT services sector is projected for steady revenue growth of 7-9% in FY26, primarily fueled by increased spending from the BFSI (Banking, Financial Services, and Insurance) sector and generative AI initiatives. As GCCs often serve their parent companies in financial services (a banking GCC report is primary IN080102), this growth indicates a significant tailwind. This is particularly relevant given the focus on AI/ML and tech within GCC mandates, enabling them to expand their service offerings and capabilities for financial clients.

forces.title: India's robust AI talent and infrastructure drive GCC growth.
forces.description: India leads globally in AI talent acquisition with a 33% annual hiring rate and significant AI skill penetration, strengthening its position as a global AI economy. The country is also investing US$200 billion in AI infrastructure, including partnerships like OpenAI with Tata Group for massive AI capacity development. This strong and growing ecosystem of talent and infrastructure provides a substantial tailwind for GCCs, enabling them to deepen their AI/ML capabilities, attract top-tier professionals, and expand their high-value services for parent companies.

forces.title: Phased AI transformation profoundly recomposes GCC workforce roles.
forces.description: GCCs are undergoing a three-stage transformation: silent restructuring (next 12 months) with 30-40% developer productivity gains and natural attrition; structural compression (years 1-3) with significant headcount reduction and emergence of new roles like AI platform engineers; and reconstitution (years 3-10) shifting to a "Global Intelligence Centre" focused on judgment and complex problem-solving. This recomposition emphasizes AI governance, agentic systems architecture, and ethical reasoning, fundamentally changing the nature of work within GCCs and requiring proactive talent management.

forces.title: GCC leaders must urgently assess AI exposure and reskill talent.
forces.description: GCC leaders face an urgent imperative to honestly map their centers' AI exposure function by function and identify the 20% of their workforce with the highest reskilling potential. Over the next 12 months, they must launch a dual operating system for "Run" and "Transform," build a pattern library for reusable AI architecture, and prepare a clear pitch to headquarters on delivering increased output at reduced cost by architecting rather than merely executing. This proactive approach is critical for navigating the AI-driven transformation effectively.

forces.title: Non-metro cities emerge as cost-effective, high-growth GCC hubs.
forces.description: Non-metro cities such as Udaipur, Vizag, Coimbatore, and Nagpur are driving over 50% IT hiring growth in H1 2025, significantly outpacing traditional hubs like Bengaluru and NCR (12-15%). These tier-II and tier-III cities attract demand in AI, cloud, and cybersecurity by offering approximately 30% cost savings. This represents a structural shift in geographical distribution, providing new opportunities for GCC expansion, talent diversification, and a more balanced regional development of the IT ecosystem in India.

forces.title: GCCs centralize data and processes for global credit management.
forces.description: Global Capability Centers (GCCs) are increasingly critical in operationalizing best practices for trade credit management by providing shared expertise, technology, and analytics. For global enterprises, GCCs consolidate data across regions, enhance real-time visibility, and improve cash flow management, supporting working capital. This centralization fosters consistency, agility, and alignment with business priorities within defined risk appetites. By acting as execution and enablement hubs, GCCs streamline global financial operations and governance for their parent companies.

forces.title: AI drives headcount compression, multiplies value per person across GCCs.
forces.description: Mega, mid-size, and emerging GCCs are all projected to see substantial headcount reductions due to AI, ranging from 45% to 65% over a decade, while simultaneously increasing economic value per person by 3-5x. Roles focused on judgment, AI governance, agentic orchestration, and domain AI translation will endure and emerge, regardless of center size. This necessitates a strategic focus on talent reskilling and new apprenticeship models to maintain a decisive talent advantage and elevate the overall value proposition of GCCs.

forces.title: AI automates junior work, necessitating new apprenticeship models for judgment.
forces.description: AI's automation of junior-level, repetitive tasks (potentially the bottom 30% of knowledge work) erodes traditional training grounds for developing senior judgment. To ensure a pipeline of skilled judgment workers for 2030, GCCs must deliberately design new apprenticeship models. these models should include structured rotations, mentorship focused on judgment, simulated scenarios, and intentional exposure to complexity, thereby replacing the experience lost to automation. This proactive talent development is essential for building a decisive and compounding talent advantage over decades.

forces.title: GCCs contribute significantly to net new tech job creation.
forces.description: Global Capability Centres are projected to generate 22-25% of net new white-collar tech jobs in India in 2025. Furthermore, out of 4.7 million new tech jobs projected by 2027, over 1.2 million are expected to originate from GCCs, primarily driven by advancements in Generative AI and engineering R&D. This highlights GCCs' crucial and growing role in India's tech employment landscape, attracting skilled talent and fostering innovation within the sector.

forces.title: AI shifts contracts from headcount-based to outcome-based models.
forces.description: AI-driven productivity gains (20-40%) in the IT industry are leading clients to demand outcome-based contracts, rather than traditional "per-FTE" or headcount-based models. Companies are adapting by offering fixed-price, subscription, and usage-based deals. This structural shift in pricing and delivery models will profoundly impact GCCs, which historically have often been linked to headcount. GCCs must now strategically demonstrate tangible value and results more explicitly to align with these evolving client expectations and secure new mandates.

viewpoints.title: AI's cognitive impact accelerates inevitable, profound GCC sector transformation.
viewpoints.description: KPMG views AI's impact on GCCs as an inevitable and accelerated transformation, drawing parallels to past major technology shifts like mainframe to client-server. Unlike previous transitions, AI directly affects cognitive work, driving rapid and profound changes in operational models. The absorption, compression, and reconstitution phases are already in motion, evidenced by AI tools automating routine tasks and boosting developer productivity. This transition demands that GCCs proactively adapt and redefine their operational models, emphasizing judgment-intensive roles and strategic thinking rather than just execution, to remain globally competitive and relevant.

viewpoints.title: GCCs are strategic hubs for data-driven, automated credit management.
viewpoints.description: EY emphasizes GCCs' role as strategic hubs, acting as execution and enablement centers for global enterprises' credit management. They support consistent adoption of credit policy frameworks by leveraging digital and analytical capabilities. Through centralizing processes, platforms, and controls, GCCs translate policy intent into disciplined, scalable practices. This includes applying advanced analytics for actionable credit insights and embedding automation, ultimately transforming credit management into a data-driven enabler of sustainable business performance and governance.

viewpoints.title: Future GCCs to be strategic brains, moving from execution to intelligence.
viewpoints.description: KPMG anticipates that future GCCs will become strategic brains for global enterprises, shifting their mandate from large-scale execution to core intelligence. The workforce will be more specialized and significantly more valuable per person as AI fulfills efficiency promises. GCCs that act as first movers in this transformation will define the next generation of global capability. This window for leadership, measured in quarters, demands quick adaptation to leverage AI for higher-value activities and secure a decisive competitive advantage for their parent companies.

viewpoints.title: AI to redefine GCCs, shifting from headcount to value creation focus.
viewpoints.description: KPMG suggests GCCs must embrace redefinition, moving from headcount-driven models to focus on value created per person. While AI may significantly reduce headcount by 25-35% in three years and 55-65% in five to ten years for current scopes, it can simultaneously generate three to five times more economic value per person. This transformation is fundamental, shifting GCCs into "Global Intelligence Centres" where AI handles execution and humans own judgment and accountability. Leaders treating this purely as a cost-cutting exercise risk compromising their strategic relevance and missing the opportunity to reimagine the center's mandate.

viewpoints.title: GCCs are crucial for strategic trade credit policy and business growth.
viewpoints.description: EY highlights GCCs as instrumental in driving strategic growth and liquidity through effective trade credit policy. They are seen as essential for enabling and monitoring robust policies that align risk, cash flow, and growth. By centralizing data, standardizing processes, and deploying real-time analytics, GCCs empower smarter, more scalable credit decisions. This elevates their role beyond merely an internal control mechanism, establishing them as a crucial strategic tool for global enterprises to manage financial health and capitalize on market opportunities.

demand_drivers.description: The proliferation and integration of Generative AI capabilities create new roles and expand existing ones within GCCs, driving demand for specialized talent.
Increased investment and focus on engineering research and development within GCCs lead to the creation of new high-value tech jobs.

market_sizing.methodology: Projection that GCCs will generate a percentage of net new white-collar tech jobs.

demand_drivers.description: Integration of AI capabilities across software services enhances offerings and efficiency, stimulating demand for exports.
India's large and skilled IT talent pool, including that within GCCs, remains a critical factor in driving software services exports.
GCCs contribute to the overall software services ecosystem by performing tech, analytics, AI/ML, and product engineering, thereby driving export growth.
Strategic alliances and partnerships focus on delivering high-value solutions, which boosts software services export revenue.

market_sizing.methodology: Projection of India's software services exports, with GCCs identified as a key driver for this growth.
